add_nodes.title: Megawatt-class compute satellites fly
add_nodes.description: A compute satellite with at least 1 MW of solar power flies and operates. That is four times the 250 kW Starmind design, with roughly 4,000-6,000 m2 of array and a high-voltage power bus.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Starmind's design point rose from 150 kW peak (Jun 2026) to 250 kW peak (Aug 2026); Musk said on Oct 1 2026 that each spacecraft carries over 250 kW of solar and the rack runs near 250 kW average. SpaceX's Sep 16 2026 FCC response bounds each satellite under 4,000 kg, 200 m2 of radiator and 1,500 m2 of solar. Starcloud-3 (~200 kW) is designed for Starship. 33FG estimates that holding a 256-expert model inside one 72-GPU satellite costs up to 44% of serving output (Jul 2026). No flight-dated compute satellite above about 250 kW was found as of Oct 2026.
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not an AI-math implication in its timing: satellite size is a SpaceX design choice on the hardware clock, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. Cheap launch removes the reason to keep satellites small, and a larger satellite holds more GPUs inside one coherent domain, which cuts the penalty of splitting a model across satellites (up to 44% of serving output for one 72-GPU satellite, 33FG). At 1 MW a 250 V bus would carry 4,000 A, so the design pulls in 300-800 V buses (materials-wbg-rad-hard-power, struct-hv-power-bus-stability) and 4,000-6,000 m2 deployable arrays whose shape and loads must be predicted (struct-deployment-mechanics). That array is 1.6-2.4 times the ISS total (about 2,500 m2) on one free-flyer. These are the AI-math inputs, all soft. A 1 MW satellite falls outside the filed per-satellite envelope (4,000 kg, 200 m2 radiator, 1,500 m2 solar) by about 3-4 times, so it needs an FCC modification; the Gen2 amendment took about 16 months to a partial grant. Starlink's major size steps took 3-4 years each (V1 2019, V2 mini 2023, V3 2026). Chain (S2): first Starmind flights 2028 -> yearly generations from 2030 -> a MW-class design after two generations of telemetry -> FCC modification and array qualification -> first flight 2033. S3 is a year earlier through faster generations. Bands (judgment): Medium by 2035 in S2-S4 because SpaceX's stated architecture is ten-satellite formation clusters of 250 kW satellites and no filing covers MW-class satellites; S1 Low.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: SpaceX may keep satellites near 250 kW and scale by numbers and formation flying, as Starlink did. Software that shrinks the single-satellite penalty would remove the main reason to go bigger.
add_nodes.signpost: A Starmind version or competing design above 500 kW announced with a flight date; a SiC or GaN power stage above 300 V named on a compute satellite.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S2 is 2033 and S3 and S4 2032 because a 1 MW satellite needs an FCC modification and 4,000-6,000 m2 of deployable array. S4 equals S3 because array deployment, power-part qualification and the FCC modification bind, and none is labor.

add_nodes.title: 10 GW of compute operating in orbit
add_nodes.description: Orbital data centers with at least 10 GW of combined power operate in orbit, about 40,000 satellites at 250 kW or fewer larger ones. At 10,000-18,000 t per GW that is 100,000-180,000 t, about 700-1,800 Starship flights at 100-150 t to low orbit, and more to dawn-dusk orbit, where each flight carries roughly 20-30% less (assumption).
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Orbital compute is at kilowatt scale. Musk has suggested Starship could support about 10 GW a year of space compute in the 2030s and projected 300-500 GW a year later (Nov 2025); he names chip and packaging supply as the main limit. SpaceXAi's S-1 (May 2026) describes Terafab, a captive chip fab in Grimes County, Texas, with Tesla and Intel on Intel 14A; land clearing began in Aug 2026. Beijing Astro-Future has proposed 16 GW of dawn-dusk orbital data centers. Anthropic and SpaceX said in May 2026 that they are interested in jointly developing multiple GW of orbital compute. Approved Starship site caps total about 145 launches a year (Starbase 25, LC-39A 44, SLC-37 76). Mach33's Launch Keystone reference case (Sep 2026) launches 38,600 t of SpaceX's own compute in 2030 and 108,000 t in 2032, passing 10 GW during 2032 at today's mass per GW (calculation). That needs about 700-1,100 compute flights in 2032 alone, about three times the 300 heavy flights a year the model's trunk first reaches in 2032-33. Mach33 is a single commercial forecaster (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous anchor on launch, satellite production, chip supply and capital, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply. At 16,000-18,000 t per GW today, or about 10,000 t at 100 kW/t, 10 GW is 100,000-180,000 t: about 700-1,800 Starship flights at 100-150 t to low orbit, and more to dawn-dusk orbit, where each flight from Florida carries roughly 20-30% less (assumption). Only the Florida pads reach these orbits; Starbase cannot fly south. At a third to a half of 300 flights a year and 100-150 t per flight, compute gets 0.6-2.3 GW a year. Chain (S3): 1 GW in 2031 -> 300+ heavy flights a year from 2032 (capability-35-heavy-cadence-300) -> cadence keeps growing by about 100 flights a year -> compute takes about half -> Starship V4 lifts about 150 t to dawn-dusk orbit and new satellites reach 100 kW/t -> 3-4 GW a year by 2034-35 -> 10 GW in 2035. Every link is an upside case. S2 runs a year behind on cadence and reaches 10 GW only after 2035. A rough simulation on the trunk's launch clock (calculation, ranges as above) puts a central case near 5-6 GW at end-2035 in S3 and 4-5 GW in S2. Chips and packaging co-bind: about 2.9 million GPU packages at 250 kW per 72-GPU satellite. Capital is large but reachable: Mach33's base case puts orbital capex at $46B per GW, falling toward $24B over a decade, so 10 GW is roughly $240-460B (a single commercial forecaster's model). Mach33's own reference reaches 10 GW in 2032, but on a launch clock about three times faster than the model's trunk. AI math is second-order: hotter chips, lighter radiators and right-sized radiation mitigation cut launched mass by a few percent to about 10%. S4 gets no credit. Robot-built pads and propellant plants (robo-earth-pads-plants, S4 2033) add some flights in 2034-35, worth roughly 0.2-2 GW by end-2035 (calculation); that leaves S4 at Low, and airspace, approvals, chips and capital do not compress. Satellite and array lines already run ahead of flights. Bands (judgment): S3 and S4 Low by 2035; S2 and S1 Speculative, after 2035.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: AI mathematics could vanish from the chain without moving this node by more than months: launch cadence, chip supply and capital set the date. If terrestrial power and permits ease, orbital compute may stall well below 10 GW.
add_nodes.signpost: Heavy flights above 300 a year with compute taking about half, by 2033; Starship V4 flying about 200 t; SpaceX reporting several GW deployed by end-2033; Starmind satellites flying Terafab chips.

add_nodes.title: A large AI model is trained in orbit
add_nodes.description: An AI lab releases or deploys a model whose main training run, at least 1e26 FLOP, ran mainly on orbital compute.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Starcloud trained a small language model on one H100 in orbit within 38 days of its Nov 2025 launch. Anthropic and SpaceX said in May 2026 that they are interested in multiple GW of orbital compute, citing ground constraints on training and inference. 33FG argues that high orbits suit asynchronous training and low orbits suit inference (Dec 2025). No multi-satellite training run has been reported.
add_nodes.why: Training uses the most power and tolerates latency, so it fits orbit well, and Anthropic named it among its reasons. It is also where radiation errors cost most: a silent error can corrupt weeks of work. That is where validated error rates (materials-see-system-models) and proven fault-tolerance bounds (materials-verified-fault-tolerance) earn their keep. A 1e26 FLOP run needs on the order of 100 NVL72-class satellites for about a month (calculation at about 40% utilization, assumption), about 25 MW, a few percent of a fleet near 1 GW. It spans several ten-satellite clusters (struct-formation-compute-clusters) joined by laser links and low-communication training methods. SpaceXAi runs both the fleet and an AI lab, and an announced run in orbit helps sell orbital compute. Chain (S3): clusters 2029 -> several hundred MW in orbit in 2031 -> the operator's own lab runs a 100-satellite job and releases the model in 2031. S2 is a year later, when its fleet nears 1 GW. Bands (judgment): High by 2035 in S3 and S4, where 1 GW is High; Medium in S2, where the fleet itself is less certain and labs may not say where a model trained; S1 Low.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Labs may keep their largest runs on the ground, where interconnect is denser and failed parts are easy to swap, and use orbit for inference. That limits frontier-scale runs; a 1e26 run needs only a few percent of the fleet. Even then AI mathematics moves the date by months, since fleet size and links bind.
add_nodes.signpost: A lab states that a released model's main training run ran in orbit; a training job spanning 50 or more compute satellites reported by 2032.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. A 1e26 FLOP run needs about 100 satellites, a few percent of a 1 GW fleet, and the operator runs its own lab, so S3 and S4 are High by 2035 and S2 Medium. S4 equals S3 because the S3 year is 2031.

add_nodes.title: Orbital compute at scale beyond dawn-dusk orbits
add_nodes.description: At least 100 MW of compute operates in orbits other than dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, such as inclined low orbits, medium Earth orbit or high Earth orbit.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Starmind, Starcloud and Suncatcher designs use dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, which gives near-continuous sunlight, needs only ~100 um of coverglass and keeps array loss under 1% a year (33FG, Dec 2025). 33FG estimates the dawn-dusk band is about 1% of usable low-orbit volume; in medium Earth orbit, belt exposure drives coverglass to ~700 um and array loss to ~3% a year.
add_nodes.why: Dawn-dusk orbits give near-continuous sun and mild radiation, so early fleets stay there. Two forces could move 100 MW elsewhere: crowding of the dawn-dusk band, which 33FG puts at about 1% of usable low-orbit volume, as fleets pass several GW; and operators choosing high orbits for asynchronous training (33FG). Inclined low orbits put batteries through about 5,500 eclipse cycles a year; higher orbits raise array loss from under 1% to about 3% a year and raise chip error rates. Here the branch's AI-math side lanes pay off: validated workload-level error rates (materials-see-system-models), proven fault-tolerance bounds (materials-verified-fault-tolerance) and model-based battery qualification (materials-battery-life-qual) let operators size shielding, batteries and mitigation before flight data exist. A tranche outside dawn-dusk orbit needs a new FCC filing or modification, since SpaceX's Jan 2026 application covers 500-2,000 km sun-synchronous orbits only. Chain (S2): dawn-dusk fleets pass several GW in 2034 -> a first tranche in another orbit, authorized and flown in 2035. S3 and S4 are a year earlier. Bands (judgment): Low by 2035 in S2-S4 because larger satellites let dawn-dusk shells hold more power and no operator has filed for another orbit; S1 Speculative.

patch.thesis: SpaceX's launch, hardware and capital clock paces orbital compute. Base case: 100-kW-class satellites fly about 2028, 1 GW is Low by 2031 and Medium by 2035, and 10 GW comes after 2035. AI math adds a few percent; arrays and chip temperatures matter more. Robots (S4) change nothing here: launch binds.
patch.reader_hook: A gigawatt of orbital compute is about 4,000 Starmind-class satellites and 110-180 Starship flights. Ten gigawatts needs about 700-1,800 flights at low-orbit payloads, and more to dawn-dusk orbit, where each flight carries roughly 20-30% less (assumption). That is two to six years of every flight at the 300 a year the model expects in the early 2030s. Qualifying chips to run about 30 C hotter saves about 1,900 t per GW (33FG model).
